families.name: Kowloon Walled City: the fused block
families.mark: One continuous 10-14 storey mass with no gaps: 350 buildings fused into a single block, its alleys tunnels under it, its roof a separate village of aerials, tanks, ladders and children, an aircraft skimming overhead.
refs: Kowloon Walled City (Wikipedia): area 210 x 120 m, ~350 buildings, 13-14 storey limit (Kai Tak), 23 m2 flats, alleys 1-2 m, 8 municipal water pipes, 77 wells, roofs with aerials/tanks/ladders
Greg Girard & Ian Lambot, City of Darkness (1993), interview: low dripping alleys, pipes overhead, rooftop air
The Japanese survey cross-section (Kowloon City Expedition, H. Kani; drawn by H. Terasawa), annotated scan
Metropolis: how the vertical village came to be
Rare historical photos of the Walled City
Gwulo: Kowloon City, a brief history
history: 1847: a Qing fort with a stone wall 4 m high and 4.6 m thick round ~2.6 ha (the yamen at its centre).
1943: the wall pulled down for Kai Tak's runway; 1947 ~2,000 squatters in one-storey huts.
1950: a fire destroys 2,500 huts; rebuilt as 2-4 storey brick and concrete.

1960s-70s: developers combine plots and pour 10-14 storey reinforced-concrete towers without permits, each new tower built hard against the last, some on top of older ones; light only from the gaps between towers.

late 1970s-80s: maximum size, the block fused; upper floors widen out over the alleys; caged balconies; rooftop huts, pigeon lofts and tanks; the roof a separate public level crossed by ladders and planks.
Kai Tak's approach 800 m south capped it at 13-14 storeys: the roofline is almost flat -- one plateau.

families.name: Korean hillside villages: daldongne, Gamcheon and the rooftop room
families.mark: Terraced cubes of concrete stacked up a steep slope so every roof is a view, pastel boxes with blue and green flat roofs and water tanks, a rooftop room (oktapbang) on many, and long stairs with no streets.
refs: Gamcheon: refugees' hillside terraces, every house with a view, 148-step 'Star Stairs'
JoongAng Daily: life in rooftop rooms (oktapbang)
history: 1950s: Korean War refugees build shacks of scrap wood, rocks and corrugated iron on steep hills.
1970s-80s: rebuilt as 1-3 storey concrete-block and brick houses on the same terraces.
2009-: artists paint them pastel; murals, sculptures; rooftop rooms and green-painted waterproofed roofs.
